For any reasonable parent who also uses physical discipline, a toddler's tantrum is in no way a reason for such punishment. It seems that some people believe that physical discipline is the first option for punishment when, in reality, it should be a last resort.

Physical discipline should be reserved for repeated and serious misbehavior only. A child crying is a natural part of their development. Most of the time, it should simply be ignored to demonstrate that it has no effect.

Physical discipline should never be administered in haste or anger. If you cannot control your emotions when dealing with a child, you have issues that extend beyond parenting. My own parents used physical discipline, and it was likely the only form of punishment that truly resonated with me. They approached it in a way that was appropriate, measured, and effective.

I was often sent to my room to allow my parents a moment to calm down; one should never administer discipline when angry and should never let that anger show during the process. The anticipation of the discipline was far worse than the act itself. Knowing it was coming and being unable to prevent it was the most difficult part.

My father typically handled the discipline. He would sit me down and discuss what had happened, what I had done, and why I was being punished. I would, of course, try to talk my way out of it, but he understood that if I managed to escape the punishment through my words, it would be a lesson lost.

He would administer the discipline, and then it was over. I would be upset, and he would leave so I could calm down. Once I was less angry, my parents would both give me a hug and reassure me of their love.

This is how physical discipline should be carried out. It establishes a foundation for a system of punishment that is not abusive but is certainly effective. There is no need to harm or mistreat your child.

This depends a lot on the distance raced and the speed you plan to achieve.

Let's say you are racing to 120 MPH over an unknown distance starting at a 35 MPH roll.

You both have similar sports cars from the same model year. You have the stock gear ratio while your competitor upgraded to a higher performance gear ratio. The engine redlines at approximately 6800 RPM.

The race starts like this.

You - 1st gear at 5272 RPM 
Competitor - 2nd gear at 4339 RPM

You are in your power band while your competitor is at the start of theirs.

You accelerate in 1st gear and shift at 45 MPH, leading your competitor who is accelerating in 2nd gear with a 9.96:1 ratio compared to your 12.10:1 ratio.

As you shift, your competitor gains on you due to your car having only an 8.04:1 ratio versus their now 9.96:1 ratio. You reach the top of your 2nd gear at 68 MPH while your competitor has to shift to 3rd at 55 MPH, allowing you to gain on them as they are at a disadvantage in gearing.

This back-and-forth continues with each shift as the gear ratios change in each other's favor. The car with the lower gear ratio will likely win in the end as it reaches 120 MPH in 4th gear while the car with the higher gear ratio has to shift to 5th after 101 MPH.

RAID 1 in theory doesn't require any calculation, just a fork so data is duplicated. If your controller is good it can also use both disks to increase read speed like a striped array.

RAID 5 and 6 are both parity calculated configurations and require a calculation of the data bits as it writes the parity bit. This calculation can hurt performance on a RAID 5 and can get even worse on a RAID 6.

RAID 10 is a nested configuration of striped and mirrored arrays. Instead of having parity, it uses 50% of the space as a duplicate and the other 50% as a striped array. This gives a ~100% performance boost over a single disk with little overhead as there are no parity calculations. The downside is that two paired drives failing still compromises the array, unlike a RAID 6 where three drives have to fail.

The biggest issue with face up is not that it has any trouble getting air through it, it's that it recycles all its air over and over getting hotter each time it goes through; having a box fan blowing in the room to circulate the air will resolve the problem as well.
Had a vertical server from the 1950s, turned my closet into a hot box, flipped it over and cooled the server substantially.
Wasn't really an issue when mounted face down, it was warmer but that air got expelled and the server sucked up cold air from the floor, mainly it was just the recycling.

What are you talking about lol? This has nothing to do with push vs pull; it's all about the fact that hot air rises... so the server blows out hot air from the bottom, it rises, then that hot air gets sucked right back into the intake and the cycle repeats. This cycle over time creates a feedback loop of heat that either overheats a heavily used server or significantly reduces its lifespan. Flipping it face down resolves all of these issues as the hot air flows up away from the intake and the intake sucks air from the coldest part of the room.
